analysis.one_liner: Requires all new cars to come with technology that detects and stops drunk drivers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committee without a vote, but a nearly identical mandate for anti-drunk-driving technology became law later in 2021 in the bipartisan infrastructure law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write a federal safety standard requiring every new passenger car and truck sold after the standard takes effect to carry 'advanced drunk driving prevention technology' — a passive system that monitors the driver, detects blood alcohol at or above .08, and prevents or limits the car from operating. The Transportation Department would have had 18 months to start, 3 years to propose, and 5 years to finalize the rule, with 2 to 3 more years for automakers to comply, and would have worked with manufacturers and safety advocates to speed the technology along. Drunk driving crashes kill roughly 10,000 people a year in the United States, and the bill's namesake — the Abbas family — was killed by a drunk driver. The bill itself never left committee, but the same core requirement was folded into the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted in November 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in or shares the road with new vehicles. A passive system that stops an impaired driver from operating the car addresses drunk-driving crashes at the moment they start, rather than relying on after-the-fact arrests. Families of crash victims and road-safety advocates gain a systemic fix; so do drivers who would never be caught by sobriety checkpoints.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Transportation Department to write a safety standard requiring passenger motor vehicles manufactured after the standard takes effect to be equipped with advanced drunk-driving prevention technology, defined as a passive system that monitors the driver's performance, passively detects blood alcohol at or above .08, or detects impairment and prevents or limits vehicle operation.

Sets a firm clock for the rulemaking: a proposal to start within 18 months, a proposed rule within 3 years, a final rule within 5 years, and an effective date giving manufacturers 2 to 3 years to comply — so the requirement could not sit unaddressed indefinitely.

Requires the Transportation Department to work directly with vehicle manufacturers, suppliers, safety advocates, and engineering universities to accelerate development of the technology and get it into cars for sale as soon as practicable.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers bear the cost of developing and installing the detection hardware and software, which would be passed into the price of every new vehicle. Buyers of new cars pay that cost; used-car buyers benefit later as the equipped vehicles enter the used fleet.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to every new passenger vehicle, so its equipment cost lands on all new-car buyers, including people who would never drive impaired.

The bill defines the technology to include systems that monitor driver performance and detect impairment, raising questions about how accurately such systems can distinguish genuine impairment from fatigue, illness, or medication, and about the privacy of continuous in-cabin driver monitoring — a system that misfires could lock a sober driver out of their own car.

By setting fixed statutory deadlines for a technology that was still being developed, the bill risked forcing a standard before the sensing systems were proven reliable; the final-rule provision allows the Secretary to explain in a report to Congress if the standard cannot be met under existing safety law, but the timetable itself is rigid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large: drunk-driving crashes kill thousands of Americans a year, and a passive in-car interlock attacks the problem at the source rather than through enforcement after the fact. The per-vehicle cost of added sensing technology falls quickly once production scales, so the main real risks are accuracy — a system that wrongly immobilizes sober drivers — and privacy from continuous monitoring. The bill tried to manage those risks by leaving the technical details to the Transportation Department's rulemaking process. On balance a strong public-safety trade, with the caveat that rigid deadlines for unproven technology can backfire.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee on the day after introduction, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened before the 117th Congress ended — though the same drunk-driving-prevention mandate passed into law that November inside the bipartisan infrastructure bill.

narrative.text: Introduced March 23, 2021 by Rep. Debbie Dingell, joined by Rep. Tom Rice and Rep. David McKinley, with eight cosponsors total (six Democrats and two Republicans).
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce; that is the last action the bill ever received.
No version of the bill was ever reported out of committee, scheduled for a floor vote, or voted on in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

A version of this requirement — directing the Transportation Department to mandate passive impaired-driving prevention technology in new vehicles — was enacted separately in the bipartisan infrastructure law of November 2021, with a longer compliance timeline than this bill's.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers came out ahead of this specific bill's timetable: the drunk-driving-prevention mandate they faced became law through the 2021 infrastructure bill with a later deadline than this bill's five-year rulemaking clock, giving them more time to develop the sensing systems. Road-safety advocates also ultimately got the policy they wanted, just on a slower track.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers got more time to comply

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and routed it to a subcommittee; never reported it out, held no markup on it, and never sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — one of the three introducing members and two of the eight cosponsors were Republicans — and no member is recorded as opposing the bill; it simply was never given committee action.

industries.note: The bill forces every passenger-vehicle maker to engineer, install, and certify passive alcohol-detection and driver-monitoring systems, costs that would flow into new-car prices. Automakers had no recorded role in this bill's fate, but a mandate with a shorter compliance clock costs them more than the later timeline they ultimately received.

The bill directs the Transportation Department to work with suppliers and manufacturers to speed development of the detection technology, effectively creating a mandated market for in-vehicle alcohol-sensing systems. Every car sold becomes a customer.

Buyers would pay somewhat more per new vehicle for the added hardware, while gaining protection against impaired operation of the car they and their families ride in. The bill's definition includes continuous driver monitoring, which brings accuracy and privacy tradeoffs for the buyer.
